source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: A formal model. The chance that a significant claim is true (PPV) depends on pre-study odds R, power 1-beta, alpha and bias u. Without bias PPV = (1-beta)R / (R - beta*R + alpha).
numbers: With alpha=0.05. PPV above 0.5 needs (1-beta)R > alpha. Example: 60% power, pre-study odds 1e-4 (schizophrenia gene search): with bias u=0.10 the post-study probability is only 4.4e-4.
quote: Research is not most appropriately represented and summarized by p-values
limits: Pure theory with assumed inputs for R, power and bias; no field-wide data. Later work disputes the size of the false-finding rate.
agent_relevance: A pass on one test is weak evidence when the prior is low and many options were tried. Supports G3: fitting the given examples is not proof.

source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: Table 4 gives PPV for typical designs. Good RCTs and confirmatory meta-analyses reach 0.85. Underpowered exploratory work is far lower.
numbers: (power, R, bias u -> PPV): adequately powered RCT (0.80, 1:1, 0.10) 0.85; confirmatory meta-analysis (0.95, 2:1, 0.30) 0.85; small inconclusive-study meta-analysis (0.80, 1:3, 0.40) 0.41; underpowered phase I/II RCT (0.20, 1:5, 0.20) 0.23; poorly performed same (0.20, 1:5, 0.80) 0.17; adequately powered exploratory epidemiology (0.80, 1:10, 0.30) 0.20; underpowered exploratory (0.20, 1:10, 0.30) 0.12; massive-testing discovery research (0.20, 1:1000, 0.80) 0.0010.
limits: Illustrative scenarios, not measured field rates.
agent_relevance: An agent that searches many hypotheses or programs lowers the odds each pass is real. Budget the number of tries (G7) and demand held-out checks (G3).

source: Ioannidis (2005) Why most published research findings are false
finding: Six corollaries: smaller studies, smaller effects, more tested relationships, more design flexibility, more financial or other interest, and more teams chasing significance each lower PPV. Claimed findings may often be accurate measures of the prevailing bias.
numbers: Corollary 3 (number of tested relationships) and 4 (flexibility in designs and analysis) map directly to search over many candidates.
limits: Corollaries are derived from the model, not tested on a field-wide dataset in this paper.
agent_relevance: Flexibility in definitions is the agent's biggest risk when it can rewrite its own checks. Fix the check before seeing the answer (G3, G2).

source: Open Science Collaboration (2015) Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: 100 studies from JPSP, JEP:LMC and Psychological Science were replicated with high-powered designs. Replication effects were half the size of originals. 97 of 100 originals were significant; 36% of replications were.
numbers: 35 of 97 replications p<.05 in the original direction (36.1%, 95% CI 26.6% to 46.2%); about 89 expected if all original effects were true (mean power 0.92). Mean effect r: original 0.403 (SD 0.188), replication 0.197 (SD 0.257), Wilcoxon W=7137, P<.001. Original-replication effect correlation Spearman r=0.51. 47% of original effects inside the replication 95% CI. 39% subjectively rated replicated. Fixed-effect meta-analysis of original plus replication: 51 of 75 (68%) with CI excluding 0.
quote: Replication effects were half the magnitude of original effects
limits: One replication per study; fidelity of replications disputed (see Gilbert et al.). Replication power about 0.92, so low power alone does not explain it.
agent_relevance: The base rate for 'a published significant result reproduces' in a noisy field is about one in three. An agent should not trust its own first positive result.

source: Open Science Collaboration (2015) Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: Stronger original evidence and simple effects replicated more; interactions and social psychology replicated less.
numbers: p<.05 replications by journal: JPSP 7/31 (23%), JEP:LMC 13/27 (48%), Psych Science 7/24 (29%). Main or simple effects 23/49 (47%) vs interaction effects 8/37 (22%). Original p<.02: 26/63 (41%); .02 to .04: 6/23 (26%); above .04: 2/11 (18%). Original p<.001: 20/32 (63%). Original effect size vs success r=0.304; replication power vs success r=0.368.
limits: Correlational predictors; cognitive tasks often within-subject, so power differs from social tasks.
agent_relevance: Marginal passes are the ones that fail. The margin of a pass can be a confidence signal computed in code (G5).

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings
finding: 28 findings, preregistered with peer-reviewed protocols, each run in about half of 125 samples (15,305 participants, 36 countries and territories). About half replicated; median effect fell to a quarter of the original.
numbers: 15 of 28 (54%) significant in the original direction at p<.05; 14 (50%) at p<.0001. Median Cohen's d: original 0.60, replication 0.15. 21 (75%) smaller than original, 7 (25%) larger. 16 (57%) small (<0.20); 9 (32%) in the opposite direction.
quote: variability in the observed effect sizes was attributable more to the effect being studied than to the sample or setting
limits: 28 chosen effects, not a random sample; success judged by significance.
agent_relevance: Large effects in one lab do not guarantee the same effect elsewhere. Agent tests should use fresh samples, not the sample that produced the claim (G3).

source: Klein et al. (2018) Many Labs 2: variation in replicability across samples and settings
finding: Hidden moderators (sample and setting) explain little. Heterogeneity was modest and concentrated in effects that were real and large.
numbers: Q test: significant heterogeneity in 11 of 28 (39%) replication effects; only 1 effect with tau above .20; 8 others tau near .10. Little heterogeneity from task order, lab vs online, or WEIRD vs less-WEIRD. Of 14 supported effects, 8 had 89% to 100% of samples significant; 6 had 11% to 46%.
limits: WEIRD comparisons were exploratory; cannot say moderators never matter.
agent_relevance: The excuse 'it depends on context' rarely rescues a failed replication. Do not accept a context story without a test (G2).

source: Camerer et al. (2016) Evaluating replicability of laboratory experiments in economics
finding: 18 lab experiments from AER and QJE (2011 to 2014), replicated with at least 90% power and public analysis plans. 11 replicated; effect size 66% of original.
numbers: 11 of 18 (61.1%) significant same direction; 92% expected if all true (binomial P<.001). Mean r: replication 0.279 vs original 0.474 (Wilcoxon z=-2.98, P=.003). Original effect inside replication 95% CI: 12 (66.7%). Prediction-interval measure 83.3%. Meta-analysis of original plus replication: 14 (77.8%) significant. Prediction market mean belief 75.2% vs observed 61.1%.
limits: 18 studies; between-subject lab designs; meta-analytic figure assumes no bias in originals.
agent_relevance: Economics replicates better than psychology but still below the rate expected from reported power. Typical shrinkage is about one third.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015
finding: 21 high-profile experiments replicated in two stages (Stage 1: 90% power for 75% of the original effect; Stage 2: 90% power for 50%). 13 replicated; effect size about half.
numbers: 13 of 21 (62%) significant same direction; 12 (57%) to 14 (67%) on other indicators. Replication samples about 5x original on average. Mean relative effect size 46.2% overall; 74.5% for the 13 that replicated; 0.3% for the 8 that did not. Bayesian: true positive rate 67%, relative effect size of true positives 71%.
limits: Small number of studies; two studies replicated only after the larger Stage 2 sample.
agent_relevance: Both false positives and inflated true effects cause failure. Top-journal papers fare no better.

source: Camerer et al. (2018) Replicability of social science experiments in Nature and Science 2010-2015
finding: Peer beliefs predict replication: prediction markets and surveys were well calibrated overall.
numbers: Market mean belief 63.4% (range 23.1% to 95.5%, 95% CI 53.7 to 73.0); survey mean 60.6%; observed 61.9%. Markets and surveys highly correlated. In the economics project markets overshot (75.2% vs 61.1%).
limits: Only 21 studies; calibration differs between projects.
agent_relevance: A cheap prior is useful: keep a count in code of how often similar claims held up, and discount new claims by it.

source: Head et al. (2015) The extent and consequences of p-hacking in science
finding: Text-mined p-values from all PubMed open-access papers (Results and Abstracts, 14 disciplines). Found evidence of real effects and also of p-hacking: an excess of p-values just under .05.
numbers: Share of significant p-values in the upper bin (.025 to .05): Results 0.257 (CI .254 to .259), Abstracts 0.262, so right-skewed (real effects). P-hacking test (bin .045-.05 vs .04-.045): estimated proportion 0.546 in Results, p<.001, n=14 disciplines.
limits: Text mining includes p-values not tied to the main hypothesis. Authors conclude the p-hacking effect is weak relative to real effects in meta-analyses.
agent_relevance: p-hacking is common but small per study. The larger danger is selection among many options. Fix the grading rule before generating (G3).

source: Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn (2011) False-positive psychology
finding: Simulations and two real experiments show that undisclosed flexibility in data collection and analysis makes false-positive rates far above the nominal 5%. They propose six author requirements and four reviewer guidelines.
numbers: Abstract only (Europe PMC). Per-practice rates and experiment N not verified this session.
quote: a researcher is more likely to falsely find evidence that an effect exists than to correctly find evidence that it does not
limits: Full text not opened; pull numbers from the paper before use.
agent_relevance: Every free choice (metric, filter, retry) inflates false passes. Count and freeze such choices before the check runs (G3, G7).

source: Franco, Malhotra & Simonovits (2014) Publication bias in the social sciences: unlocking the file drawer
finding: Tracked a known population of 221 TESS survey experiments. Null results are much less often published, mostly because authors never write them up.
numbers: Strong results are 40 percentage points more likely to be published and 60 percentage points more likely to be written up than null results (abstract).
limits: Abstract only; stage-wise percentages not verified.
agent_relevance: Failures are dropped before anyone sees them. An agent should log every failed attempt and its output, not only the winner (G2, G6).

source: John, Loewenstein & Prelec (2012) Measuring the prevalence of questionable research practices with incentives for truth telling
finding: Survey of over 2,000 psychologists with incentives for honest answers. Questionable research practices were surprisingly common and may be the prevailing norm.
numbers: Abstract only: over 2,000 respondents; three estimation methods combined; incentives raised admissions most for the less defensible practices. Percentages not verified.
limits: Self-report; admission is not proof of harm.
agent_relevance: Pressure shapes what gets reported. An agent graded on a reported score has the same pressure; score it by running held-out checks (G3, G8).

source: Button et al. (2013) Power failure: why small sample size undermines the reliability of neuroscience
finding: Low power cuts the chance of finding true effects and the chance that a significant result is true; it also inflates effect estimates. Average power in neuroscience is very low.
numbers: Abstract only. The median power figure was not verified this session.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Winner's curse: the best of many noisy trials is biased high. Report the held-out score, not the selected one (G3).

source: Gilbert, King, Pettigrew & Wilson (2016) Comment on 'Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science'
finding: A critique. It claims the OSC paper has three statistical errors and that the data are consistent with high reproducibility.
numbers: Abstract only. The specific corrected rates were not verified.
limits: Disputed; the two sides use different definitions of success, and the OSC authors replied.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition for the headline rate: a 'failure' may be a protocol mismatch. Compare against a fixed written protocol (G3).

source: ASA (2016) Statement on statistical significance and p-values (press release)
finding: The American Statistical Association gave six principles: p-values show incompatibility with a model, not the probability the hypothesis is true; no decisions on a threshold alone; full reporting needed; a p-value is not effect size; by itself not good evidence.
numbers: Six principles, 7 March 2016. Alternatives named: estimation with intervals, Bayesian methods, likelihood ratios or Bayes factors, decision-theoretic modelling, false discovery rates.
quote: The p-value was never intended to be a substitute for scientific reasoning
limits: This file is the press release, not the Wasserstein and Lazar paper.
agent_relevance: An agent's pass rule should report size and margin, and log all tests run, not a bare pass (G3).

source: Starace et al. (2025) PaperBench: evaluating AI's ability to replicate AI research
finding: Agents must replicate 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight/Oral papers from scratch, graded on 8,316 rubric items by an LLM judge. Best agent 21.0%.
numbers: Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) 21.0%; o1 13.2%; other models under 10%. Human ML PhDs on a 3-paper subset: 41.4% (best of 3, 48 h) vs o1 26.6%. CodeDev variant with IterativeAgent: o1-high 24.4 +-0.7, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 16.1 +-0.1, o3-mini-high 8.5 +-0.8; o1 with 36 h limit 26.0.
quote: all models apart from Claude 3.5 Sonnet frequently finished early
limits: Mostly LLM-judge grading (o3-mini judge about $66 per run, validated on JudgeEval).
agent_relevance: Agents often finished early, claiming success or giving up, and did not plan. Supports code-checked completion, not self-report (G6, G2).

source: Siegel et al. (2024) CORE-Bench: computational reproducibility agent benchmark
finding: 270 tasks from 90 papers (CS, social science, medicine): run the authors' code and answer questions about the output. Best agent: 60% easy, 57.78% medium, 21.48% hard.
numbers: CORE-Agent+GPT-4o 60.00 / 57.78 / 21.48%. CORE-Agent+GPT-4o-mini 44.44 / 32.59 / 16.30%. AutoGPT+GPT-4o 35.56 / 37.78 / 6.67%. AutoGPT+GPT-4o-mini 8.89 / 2.22 / 2.22%. Test split, pass@1; CORE-Agent mean of 3 runs, AutoGPT 1 run.
limits: A task passes only if all questions are correct; agents were tuned on the train split.
agent_relevance: Task-specific scaffolding tripled hard-level accuracy (6.67 to 21.48 with the same model). Scaffold design, not just model size, drives reproduction skill.

source: Beel, Kan & Baumgart (2025) Evaluating Sakana's AI Scientist
finding: Independent evaluation of an end-to-end AI scientist. Weak literature review, frequent coding failures, misleading results, hallucinated numbers.
numbers: 5 of 12 proposed experiments (42%) failed from coding errors; each iteration added only 8% more characters of code; median 5 citations per paper, only 5 of 34 from 2020 or later; micro-batching for SGD wrongly judged novel; one energy-efficiency experiment reported accuracy gains while using more compute.
limits: Small sample (12 experiments); system as of 2024.
agent_relevance: Automated reports can look fine to a quick reviewer. Check claims by re-running, not reading (G2, G8).

source: Aher, Arriaga & Kalai (2023) Using LLMs to simulate multiple humans and replicate human subject studies
finding: Turing Experiments: simulate a sample of participants with LLMs and compare to classic findings. Ultimatum Game, garden path and Milgram were replicated with recent models; wisdom of crowds showed a hyper-accuracy distortion.
numbers: Valid generation rates across 5 models: Ultimatum 88.0 to 99.5%, Garden path 95.5 to 99.2%, Wisdom of Crowds 51.0 to 99.0%. Ultimatum run over 2,500 name pairings, with a gender effect. Larger and more aligned models give inhumanly accurate answers: median normalised estimate 1.0 with 0 IQR for LM-6, ChatGPT and GPT-4.
limits: Classic findings may sit in training data (authors wrote new items to reduce this).
agent_relevance: LLM 'participants' are too consistent. Samples from one model are not independent, which supports G4.

source: Bouthillier et al. (2021) Accounting for variance in machine learning benchmarks
finding: ML benchmark comparisons ignore variance from data sampling, initialization and hyperparameter choice. Randomising more sources with a cheaper estimator gives a 51x compute cut versus the ideal estimator.
numbers: Five deep-learning tasks. Single-point comparison and average comparison have either about 10% false positives or very low detection power (false positives under 5%); the probability-of-outperforming test with threshold gamma=0.75 gives about 5% false positives and reasonable detection.
limits: Small deep-learning models, pre-LLM; seeds are controllable there.
agent_relevance: Template for G7: compare scaffold vs plain with paired runs and a probability-of-outperforming test with a confidence interval, not one score.

source: Atil et al. (2024) Non-determinism of 'deterministic' LLM settings
finding: Five LLMs at temperature 0 on eight tasks (from MMLU and BBH), 10 runs each: none repeats accuracy or output across all tasks.
numbers: Accuracy varies by up to 15% across natural runs; gap between best and worst possible run up to 70%. New metrics TARr@N and TARa@N (total agreement rate over N runs).
limits: Eight tasks; results differ by model and API.
agent_relevance: Single-run claims of a gain are noisy. Run repeated seeds; treat a gain inside the run-to-run range as no gain (G7).

source: Dominguez-Olmedo, Hardt & Mendler-Dunner (2023) Questioning the survey responses of large language models
finding: 43 LMs (110M to 175B parameters) answered 25 American Community Survey questions. Raw answers show ordering and label bias (letter A). With randomised answer order, answers trend toward uniform random.
numbers: 43 models, 25 ACS 2019 questions; alignment scores are explained by how close a subgroup is to the uniform distribution.
limits: Multiple-choice format.
agent_relevance: LLM results hinge on prompt format. Check by shuffling options and re-scoring (G3: mutated input).

source: Open Science Collaboration (2015) Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science
finding: Original p-values were far smaller than replication p-values; the 64 non-significant replications were not explained by low power alone.
numbers: Mean p-value: original 0.028, replication 0.302. 64 of the 100 had non-significant replications. Original effect size correlates with success r=0.304.
limits: Dichotomous significance is a crude indicator; authors also give effect-size and meta-analytic indicators.
agent_relevance: Pass/fail alone hides magnitude. Log the margin and effect size of every check, not just the verdict (G3).
